subject: Computer Networking
title: The Radio Spectrum
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Radio Spectrum.

hook.text: Every wireless device — your phone, Wi-Fi, TV, GPS — shares the same limited resource: the radio spectrum.

buildup.text: The spectrum is divided into frequency bands. Each band has different properties: range, speed, and penetration.

discovery.text: Lower frequencies travel farther and penetrate walls. Higher frequencies carry more data but fade quickly.

twist.text: Governments auction spectrum licenses for billions. The 5G auction in the U.S. raised over $80 billion.

climax.text: Unlicensed bands like 2.4 GHz are free for anyone. That's why Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and microwaves all share it.

punchline.text: Spectrum is finite. Every wireless device competes for a slice.

quiz.question: Why do lower radio frequencies travel farther?
options: They penetrate obstacles better and lose less energy over distance
They carry more data per second

details.summary: The radio spectrum is the range of electromagnetic frequencies used for wireless communication, strictly regulated by governments worldwide. Different frequency bands are allocated to specific uses — cellular, Wi-Fi, TV, satellite, and more.
details.whyItMatters: Spectrum allocation determines what wireless technologies are possible and who can use them. Spectrum scarcity drives innovation, policy debates, and billion-dollar auctions that shape the wireless landscape.
takeaways: The radio spectrum is divided into licensed and unlicensed bands
Governments auction licensed spectrum to carriers for billions
Unlicensed bands like 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz enable Wi-Fi for everyone

faq.question: What is the difference between licensed and unlicensed spectrum?
faq.answer: Licensed spectrum is auctioned to specific operators who get exclusive use and protection from interference. Unlicensed spectrum like the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands can be used by anyone following power limits.

faq.question: Why are spectrum auctions so expensive?
faq.answer: Mobile operators pay billions because spectrum is finite and essential for their service. More spectrum means more capacity and faster speeds. The 2021 US C-band auction raised 81 billion dollars.
